question: A 25-year-old man presents to his primary care provider complaining of scrotal swelling. He is a college student and plays basketball with his friends regularly. Two days ago, he sustained an injury close to his thigh. He does not have any significant past medical history. Today, his vitals are normal. A focused scrotal examination reveals a firm painless lump on the right testicle which is irregular and small. Ultrasound of the scrotum reveals a vascular 0.6 x 0.5 cm testicular mass. A pelvic lymph node exam is negative. He undergoes a radical orchiectomy and subsequent histopathological examination reveals sheets of small cuboidal cells, multinucleated cells, and large eosinophilic cells with pleomorphic nuclei consistent with choriocarcinoma. Which of the following tumor marker is most likely elevated in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Presence of testicular mass on ultrasound -> Radical orchiectomy performed -> Histopathological examination reveals choriocarcinoma -> Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) most likely elevated -> 95%
enhanced_information: The patient's histopathological examination revealed choriocarcinoma, indicating that beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) is most likely elevated in this patient. This aligns with standard consensus as β-hCG is a classic tumor marker for choriocarcinoma.
analysis: Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant germ cell tumor that commonly secretes beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG). The histopathological findings of sheets of small cuboidal cells, multinucleated cells, and large eosinophilic cells with pleomorphic nuclei are consistent with choriocarcinoma. Therefore, the most likely elevated tumor marker in this patient is beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG).
